name: Schisandra chinensis
lead: Schisandra chinensis, the Chinese magnolia vine or five-flavour berry (wuweizi in Chinese, omija in Korean), is a deciduous woody vine native to forests of northern China, the Russian Far East, Korea and Japan. Its red berries are used in traditional medicine and in a Korean cordial drink, and extracts are sold as an adaptogen in the longevity and stress-resilience supplement category.[1][2][24]

People take it for the chain of effects attributed to adaptogens: better stamina and stress tolerance, and recovery, which supporters link to training consistency, sleep and a healthier-looking complexion. Researchers have described its leading lignans, such as schisandrin, deoxyschizandrin and gomisins, and laboratory studies report liver-protective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.[1][3][4][5][6][7] Plant-extract reviews of skin care also list botanical antioxidants and anti-aging agents as a general category, although schisandra itself has not been tested in trials for skin or hair appearance.[14]

Human trials of schisandra are few and small, covering muscle strength and fatigue, knee osteoarthritis, menopausal symptoms, hyperglycemia and combination adaptogen formulas.[9][10][15][16][17][18][19]

paras: The Chinese and Korean names both refer to the berry's five flavours: bitter, sweet, sour, salty and pungent.[1] Wikipedia notes the Ainu used the plant as a remedy for colds and sea-sickness, and that Koreans make the berries into the cordial omija-cha.[1] The genus was published by André Michaux in 1803, and the plant was once placed in Magnoliaceae, hence the name Chinese magnolia vine.[1]

The vine can climb 8 to 9 metres, sometimes much more, and is usually dioecious, so fruit-bearing female plants need pollen from male plants. It tolerates cold to about minus 30 degrees Celsius and flowers roughly three years after sowing.[1] The berries hang in dense clusters.[1]

Researchers in the Soviet Union studied the plant in the twentieth century as a tonic and stimulant, and a 2008 review summarises that Russian research and its uses in medicine.[2] Schisandra, together with Panax ginseng, Eleutherococcus, Rhaponticum and Rhodiola, is classed among the plant adaptogens, extracts said to raise resistance to physical load; reviews describe their use in professional sports beginning about fifty years ago and look at future applications.[24]

Botanically, it is a perennial climbing vine in the family Schisandraceae, hardy in cold temperate zones, whose stems commonly reach 8 to 9 metres as they climb trees and shrubs. Plants are usually dioecious, with separate male and female vines, and bear hanging clusters of red berries 5 to 10 mm across that usually contain one or two seeds. [1] The Chinese name wuweizi means roughly five-flavour berry, reflecting the belief that the fruit carries all five basic tastes: bitter, sweet, sour, salty and pungent. [1] The Ainu of Japan are recorded as using the plant for colds and seasickness, and the crushed leaves give off a lemon-like scent. [1] A separate species, Schisandra sphenanthera, is listed on its own in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia. [1][8]

Reviews list dibenzocyclooctadiene lignans as the characteristic constituents of the fruit and describe analytical methods that distinguish S. chinensis from S. sphenanthera.[3][8] Preclinical studies report that schisandrin has anti-inflammatory effects in cell models,[6] that schisandrin B promotes fatty-acid oxidation and reduces liver fat accumulation in a mouse model through AMPK/mTOR signalling,[7] and that pollen extract and an acidic polysaccharide reduced chemically induced liver injury in mice.[4][5] A 2008 review of Russian research covers its traditional use as a general tonic.[2]

Registered human trials are few and small. They include a 54-person randomised trial of extract on musculoskeletal biomarkers in relatively sarcopenic adults,[9] a Phase 2/3 study of omija extract in mild knee osteoarthritis (60),[10] a trial of a multi-herb formula in fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome that includes schisandra among six ingredients,[11] and a Phase 3 trial of the Shengmai San formula to prevent chemotherapy-related cardiac toxicity.[12] Another trial compared a combined Rhodiola, Schisandra and Eleutherococcus preparation with rhodiola extract and ginseng in employed middle-aged women.[13] The sources consulted give no results, and none tests an appearance outcome.

A randomized trial examined Schisandra chinensis extract on quadriceps muscle strength and fatigue in adult women, and a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial examined it for menopausal symptoms.[15][16] A single-dose placebo-controlled study of a Rhodiola, Schisandra and Eleutherococcus combination (ADAPT-232) measured cognitive functions, and a pilot trial examined the effect of adaptogens on ultraweak biophoton emission in 30 volunteers.[17][18] A 12-week trial of an omija extract and soybean mixture enrolled 80 people with raised fasting glucose.[19]

Schisandra is reported to affect drug-metabolising pathways. Laboratory research found that Wu Wei Zi and licorice (Gan Cao) activate the pregnane X receptor and increase clearance of warfarin in rats, a basis for caution about herb-drug interactions.[20] Herbal supplements generally lack the monitoring that medicines have, and no trial has tested its safety against appearance-related uses.

On T Nation threads, schisandra appears as one ingredient among many in liver-support and hormone-support supplement stacks, and posters list it with lemon balm, rhodiola and eleuthero when discussing adaptogens.[21][22][23]

card.summary: The five-flavour berry of Chinese and Russian tonic tradition; liver and antioxidant lab data, nothing on looks.
card.note: Human trials are few and mostly in combination formulas.

quick.overview:
Schisandra is a vine whose berries are used as a tonic in Chinese, Korean and Russian traditions and sold as an adaptogen supplement.
Laboratory studies report liver-protective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Human trials are small, often of multi-herb formulas, and none addresses appearance.
quick.mechanism: Its lignans, such as schisandrin and schisandrin B, are reported in animal and cell studies to act on inflammatory and metabolic signalling, including AMPK/mTOR pathways.
quick.risks: Safety and interaction data are limited. Product identity can vary because S. chinensis and S. sphenanthera are different species.

angle.text: Schisandra is taken as an adaptogen and liver-support herb. People who use it connect better stress resilience and recovery with better training, sleep and general appearance.
